item.title: Beyond straight lines
item.description:
Beyond straight lines#

Example 1: a building's electricity demand#

A smart meter records the power drawn by an office building. Low at night. A morning peak (about 9 am). A larger evening peak (about 7:30 pm)

A load profile like this is what an energy manager or a utility wants to predict, for example to size a solar system or plan tariffs. Energy monitoring was a survey topic.

item.title: How good is a classifier?
item.description:
How good is a classifier?#

Judging a classifier: four kinds of outcome#

model says really
TP faulty faulty true positive
FP faulty healthy false positive
FN healthy faulty false negative
TN healthy healthy true negative

Before any numbers, the vocabulary. Every later measure of quality (accuracy, recall, precision, the ROC curve) is built from these four outcomes, so students must know them by heart.

Two words name each outcome. Positive / negative = what the model said. Positive: class 1 (faulty, what we look for). Negative: class 0 (healthy)

item.title: The support vector classifier
item.description:
The support vector classifier#

When the classes overlap#

Real data overlap: no line separates them perfectly

Then the maximal margin classifier has no solution.

Support vector classifier: allow some points inside the street, or on the wrong side of the line, but pay a price for each one

Each point gets a slack variable \(\varepsilon_i\): 0 if it is on the correct side outside the street, between 0 and 1 if inside the street, above 1 if on the wrong side (ISLP 9.2.2).

input unit

acoustic noise dB

Inputs: vibration (mm/s), bearing temperature (\(^\circ\)C), motor current (A), acoustic noise (dB), running hours (h), humidity (%)

A typical condition-monitoring record. Motor current rises when a motor is overloaded or a bearing drags. Acoustic noise and running hours indicate wear. Humidity is included as an input that plays no part.

item.title: Generative models: LDA, QDA, naive Bayes
item.description:
Generative models: LDA, QDA, naive Bayes#

Probability words for the next four slides#

Word Meaning
\(\Pr(A \mid B)\) probability of \(A\) given that \(B\) is true (conditional probability)
prior \(\pi_k\) probability of class \(k\) before we look at \(X\): how common the class is
density \(f_k(x)\) how the inputs \(X\) are spread in class \(k\): high where class-\(k\) points are common
normal (Gaussian) the bell-shaped distribution, set by its mean and spread
mean \(\mu\) (“mu”) the centre of a distribution: the average
covariance \(\Sigma\) (capital “sigma”, here not a sum) the spread of each input and how inputs vary together: it sets the size, shape and tilt of the cloud of points

LDA, QDA and naive Bayes are described in the language of probability. Most students have met these words in a statistics course but may not be fluent. Go through them before the formulas.

item.title: Gradient descent
item.description:
Gradient descent#

Loss and cost: what is the difference?#

Two words that students will meet in every later lecture and in every software library, often used loosely. Fix them now.

Loss: how wrong the model is on one data point. \(\ell_i = \frac12(y_i - \hat y_i)^2\)

The loss is a number for a single reading: half its squared residual.

Cost: the average loss over all \(n\) points. One number for the whole dataset. \(J(\bb) = \frac1n\sum_i\ell_i = \frac{1}{2n}\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\)

Two proximity probes at right angles measure the position of a rotating shaft (\(x\), \(y\) in \(\mu\)m)

Eddy-current proximity probes are standard on large turbines, compressors and pumps. Plotting \(y\) against \(x\) gives the shaft's orbit.

item.title: Recurrent networks
item.description:
Recurrent networks#

Sequences: recurrent networks#

Diagram: inputs \(x_{t-3}, \dots, x_t\); hidden states connected in a chain; forecast from the last

A recurrent network reads a sequence one step at a time. Its hidden state \(h\) carries a memory of what came before, updated at every step with the same weights

item.title: SVMs in practice
item.description:
SVMs in practice#

More than two classes#

One-versus-one: fit an SVM for every pair of \(K\) classes: \(K(K - 1)/2\) SVMs. Each votes; the class with the most votes wins. (scikit-learn's SVC does this.)

One-versus-all: fit \(K\) SVMs: each class against all the others. Choose the class whose SVM is most confident

Fault type: three classes (imbalance, misalignment, bearing wear): 3 SVMs either way

\(3 \times 2/2 = 3\) pairs; and 3 one-versus-all SVMs. With 10 classes it would be 45 against 10.

When to use deep learning#

item.title: Statistical learning
item.description:
Statistical learning#

Two words from statistics: average and variance#

The next slides use the symbols \(\mathbb E\) and \(\operatorname{Var}\). Many students last met them in a first-year statistics course, so they are defined here, with an example, before they are used.

Expected value (long-run average): \(\mathbb E(Z) \approx (z_1 + z_2 + \dots + z_m)/m\) for a large number of repeats \(m\)

A random quantity \(Z\) takes a different value each time it is measured. Its expected value is the average we would get if we measured it very many times. “Approximately” because the average of a finite number of repeats is only close to it.

item.title: Assessing model accuracy
item.description:
Assessing model accuracy#

Measuring the quality of fit: the mean squared error#

Mean squared error on the training data: \(\mathrm{MSE} = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat f(x_i))^2\)

The standard score for a regression model.

item.title: Classification
item.description:
Classification#

Classification: the error rate#

For categories the MSE makes no sense. Count the mistakes instead

“Faulty minus healthy” has no meaning, so we cannot square a difference.

Error rate (fraction of wrong labels): \(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n I(y_i \neq \hat y_i)\)
